Audio-driven lip synchronization aims to match target speech through localized mouth and jaw articulation while preserving subject identity, head pose, and surrounding facial context. Naturally recorded videos provide synchronized reconstruction targets but rarely offer pairs that are matched in identity and pose yet differ primarily in speech-related articulation. Mask-based training enables reconstruction from these videos, but random-reference inputs differ from the aligned self-reference used at inference. We present LiveSync, an iterative self-training framework in which a single mask-based model generates pseudo pairs and is refined for deployment. The model is first trained on a curated real-video corpus augmented with externally generated clips covering under-represented visual conditions. A frozen checkpoint then uses independently sampled audio to generate mouth-edited references from real-video frames, copying pixels outside the edit mask from each source frame. After confidence filtering, these references are paired with aligned masked inputs and original real-frame targets. The retained pseudo pairs are mixed with real training data to refine the same model from its current weights, updating training supervision without adding inference stages. Although we instantiate the framework with a single-pass GAN-based model, the self-training strategy could in principle also be adapted to diffusion-based models. Experimental results show that LiveSync achieves leading synchronization performance on HDTF and competitive performance compared with the baselines on the AIGC-LipSync subset, while maintaining low inference latency.

Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Sihan Xu, Yuwei Niu, Xihui Liu
A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

☆ PanoBench: A Panoptic Occupancy Prediction Benchmark for Autonomous Driving
Yi Feng, Zizhan Guo, Junwu E, Yu Ma, Mengtan Zhang, Jin Wu, Wei Ye, Hanli Wang, Qijun Chen, Danwei Wang, Rui Fan
Panoptic occupancy unifies 3D geometry, semantics, and instance identities, but its development is limited by scarce instance-aware annotations. Existing benchmarks mainly provide semantic labels reconstructed from incomplete sensor observations, while panoptic datasets have limited domain coverage or annotation completeness. We introduce PanoBench, a camera-centric panoptic occupancy prediction benchmark spanning synthetic and real-world driving scenes. It combines PanoBench-CarlaOcc, PanoBench-nuScenes, and PanoBench-KITTI360 through canonical data interfaces and unified evaluation protocols, providing multi-resolution annotations with persistent instance identities. The synthetic branch derives complete panoptic geometry from simulated meshes. For real-world data, a new pipeline reconstructs backgrounds using geometric priors and topology constraints, generates foreground mesh assets from multi-frame multi-view images, and fuses them into sparse panoptic voxels. A unified valid-mask protocol evaluates complete thing instances supported by temporal observations while scoring stuff regions at the voxel level. Analyses of observation fidelity, geometric completeness, spatial continuity, and temporal consistency demonstrate the benefits of the resulting annotations over existing occupancy benchmarks. We benchmark representative methods on semantic occupancy prediction, panoptic occupancy prediction, and 4D occupancy forecasting, and study voxel resolution, synthetic-to-real transfer, and storage efficiency. These results reveal complementary strengths of volumetric and ray-based metrics and persistent challenges in real-world instance-aware prediction. PanoBench is available at https://mias.group/PanoBench.
☆ PreciseEdit: Strong Yet Stable Semantic Transport for One-Step Image Editing
Jingyi Wang, Xiao Lu
Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models enable efficient image synthesis, opening up new possibilities for interactive Web-based image editing. However, existing one-step editing methods often construct a global transport field through simple vector operations between conditional predictions. While such strong transport can effectively drive the image toward the target semantics, it may be released along unreliable directions or over non-edited regions, leading to structural distortions within the editing region and background drift elsewhere. More importantly, stabilizing the editing process through global smoothing or uniformly weakening the transport field often makes large semantic changes overly conservative. In this work, we revisit one-step image editing from the perspective of the tension between semantic strength and transport stability, and identify a key insight: strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable. What matters is whether it is applied along reliable directions and at reliable spatial locations. Motivated by this insight, we introduce PreciseEdit, a model-agnostic, training-free and inversion-free one-step editing framework that strengthens target-semantic alignment while preserving background fidelity and structural consistency. We further propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy: a higher-noise scale produces the strong target-directed transport used for actual editing, whereas a lower-noise scale jointly serves as a probe for directional agreement and spatial structure. Extensive experiments on PIE-Bench demonstrate that PreciseEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance and effectiveness on various editing tasks.

☆ ReVision: Reprogramming Image Generators for Dense Visual Perception
Yitong Yang, Yinglin Wang, Xuexin Liu, Wei Chen, Zhaoyang Xu, Jiaxin Lin, Rui Chen, Shuting He, Kai Wang
Recent image generators exhibit rich visual priors that can support dense visual perception. However, existing approaches typically encode multiple perception tasks into a shared parameterization, making joint training sensitive to the mixture and weighting of heterogeneous data and prone to cross-task interference. To address this issue, we introduce ReVision, an instruction-conditioned parameter generation framework built on a frozen multimodal understanding model and a frozen image generator. Given an image and a free-form instruction, the understanding model jointly encodes them into a multimodal image--instruction representation, which a trainable parameter generator maps to transient low-rank updates for the generator. Each image--instruction pair induces a distinct set of transient prediction parameters, enabling instance-specific adaptation while both pretrained backbones remain unchanged. ReVision requires no task-specific heads, explicit task identifiers, or stored adapters. A shared RGB output interface unifies segmentation, depth estimation, and surface-normal prediction. Across diverse dense prediction benchmarks, ReVision achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods while supporting flexible task specification through natural-language instructions. Our analysis further reveals substantial gradient disagreement across tasks, highlighting the conflict introduced when heterogeneous objectives share a single parameterization. Meanwhile, the generated updates exhibit structured task- and input-dependent organization in weight space, further validating instance-level parameter generation for multi-task perception.
☆ PONDER: Learning to Generate in the Right Order
Julius Erbach, Dominik Narnhofer, Bernt Schiele, Jan Eric Lenssen, Konrad Schindler
We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78 and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 3.9\% to 56.6\%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (38.7\%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID and 96.7\% accuracy, while increasing the rethinking budget of a fixed policy yields continued improvements at inference time.

☆ TAN: A Size- and Form-Adaptive Masked-Convolution Encoder for Tissue Graphs
Jan Herschel, Anselm von Gladiss
Tissue graphs represent histology images as graphs over tissue-conforming superpixels, which keeps homogeneous tissue regions intact instead of cutting them into rectangular patches. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.
☆ When Evidence Vanishes: Distilling Visual-Evidence Dependency in Medical Vision-Language Models

Compact medical vision-language models (VLMs) can answer clinical questions correctly without reliably using the image, relying instead on question wording or learned priors. Standard knowledge distillation copies a teacher's answer preference on the original image, but it leaves unchecked whether that preference is conditional on the visual evidence required by the question. We study this missing target as medical visual evidence dependency: support for the correct answer should decrease when the matched evidence is absent. We introduce Evidence-Conditioned Dependency Distillation (ECDD), which pairs each training image with a control matched to the evidence level and distills the teacher's drop in answer margin across the pair. A lower bound objective transfers positive dependency by penalizing only shortfalls, while original-image supervision preserves task accuracy. The same formulation applies when the evidence is a queried clinical region, a surgical instrument, or whole-image visual content. Across three medical VQA settings, ECDD keeps original-image accuracy competitive with distillation and alignment baselines while making answer support more sensitive to evidence removal. Under the DME headline objective, for example, the positive-case margin response to target rather than random masking rises from 0.786 with KD to 2.023 with ECDD, while original-image accuracy differs by 0.11 points. These results suggest that medical VLM distillation should transfer both the teacher's answer preference and its dependence on visual evidence.

Atmospheric turbulence degrades image quality in long-range imaging. The degradation is generally modeled with two spatio-temporally varying components, tilt and blur. Recent unsupervised turbulence mitigation methods have demonstrated the effectiveness of representing a sharp image as an implicit neural representation (INR). However, their tilt and blur representations remain frame-dependent, and the number of optimization parameters grows with the number of input frames. To address this limitation, we propose TriINR, an unsupervised turbulence mitigation method that recovers a sharp image from multiple degraded frames. We further incorporate physical and statistical properties of atmospheric turbulence as constraints on the INRs to improve restoration accuracy. Experiments on synthesized turbulence data with three degradation strengths show that TriINR restores images more robustly across varying turbulence strengths than prior TM methods and achieves the highest accuracy among the evaluated unsupervised methods. Our method also demonstrates robustness on real long-range scenes containing additional non-ideal motion.

Shadows cast by elevated objects alter the spectral appearance and obscure the boundaries of objects in remote sensing images, thereby degrading semantic segmentation performance. Most existing approaches handle shadows as degradations to be detected and removed, requiring additional costs from dedicated networks and shadow-specific annotations. We propose ShadowCast, which takes the opposite approach: it synthesizes shadows and injects them during training for remote sensing segmentation. It extracts masks of elevated objects, such as buildings and trees, directly from the segmentation labels and estimates an image-specific cast-shadow direction cue by probing the brightness around them. It then projects synthetic shadows along the inferred cast-shadow direction, requiring no learned network and no acquisition metadata. Experiments on three widely used remote sensing benchmarks, Vaihingen, Potsdam, and LoveDA, show that ShadowCast consistently outperforms the baseline across diverse state-of-the-art segmentation architectures. Moreover, it brings additional performance gains when combined with standard augmentation and regularization techniques, indicating that stochastic shadow injection serves as a simple and complementary augmentation strategy for remote sensing segmentation.

☆ GeoReason: Bridging Logical Reasoning and Spatial Fidelity in Remote Sensing Segmentation
Cheng Fan, Han Wu, Tingzhang Luo, Minjing Dong, Yehui Tang, Jianyuan Guo
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.

To address this limitation, we investigate a human-inspired evaluation framework that avoids representations learned for unrelated tasks. Specifically, we train a generator-specific classifier to distinguish real images from samples produced by a given model and analyze its decisions using saliency maps. Across diverse benchmarks, we observe that these classifiers learn generator-specific artifacts rather than a universal notion of "fakeness", exhibiting strong accuracy and limited cross-generator transfer. This makes saliency analysis particularly informative: the resulting attribution maps highlight visual cues and structural irregularities characteristic of each model's outputs. By combining classification accuracy and saliency information, we obtain a composite score aligned with human judgments, without relying on large pretrained backbones and using only real and generated samples from the evaluated model.

Qualitative SEM retrieval illustrates recovery to qualified interiors without requiring exact reference-coordinate matching.

Second, we develop an intention-aware agentic prompt enhancement (PE) module that translates diverse user requests into detailed content and layout specifications. Together, they enable MOSS-Image to generate text-rich and layout-coherent images. We further introduce LongLongTextBench (LLTB) for evaluating long-form English and Chinese text rendering, and RealLayoutArena (RLA) for end-to-end layout-rich generation. MOSS-Image achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-weight models on LLTB, with an average text coverage of 96.3%. On RLA, MOSS-Image ranks second in the end-to-end system comparison, while its backbone ranks first among generators evaluated with shared enhanced prompts. We will release the model, training recipe, and evaluation framework to support further research and promote the text-to-image community.

☆ UniPolar: Joint Image and Polarimetric Restoration under Compound Degradations via Physical Consistency Learning
Yang Jin, Guangyu Guo, Linghao Shen, Binglu Wang
Polarimetric image restoration aims to recover polarization angle images and reliable polarimetric quantities from degraded observations. Beyond visual fidelity, it also requires preserving the physical relationships underlying reliable polarimetric estimation. However, existing methods typically address either device- or environment-induced degradations in isolation, limiting their applicability to color polarization filter array (CPFA) imaging, where both often coexist. Such compound degradations jointly perturb image intensities and cross angle polarization differences. Consequently, improved image fidelity alone does not necessarily ensure accurate Stokes, DoLP, and AoLP recovery. To address this challenge, we propose UniPolar, a coupled Image Stokes framework for joint image polarimetric restoration from compound-degraded CPFA observations. Specifically, UniPolar employs two complementary streams to reconstruct four polarization-angle images and directly predict Stokes difference components. To coordinate these streams, Degradation Conditioned Cross Domain Interaction combines Dual Domain Frequency Interaction for frequency selective evidence exchange with Degradation Conditioned Modulation for condition adaptive feature correction. Furthermore, at the output level, Image Stokes Physical Consistency Learning aligns image derived and directly predicted Stokes components while regularizing angular fidelity and the physical feasibility of DoLP. On the compound-degradation benchmark, UniPolar achieves average image and DoLP PSNR of 31.522 dB and 24.097 dB, respectively, with an average AoLP error of 16.833 degree. These results underscore the importance of jointly considering visual fidelity and polarimetric reliability, offering a physically grounded perspective on learning based restoration under compound degradations.

These differences were small relative to between-patient variability. In the separate adaptive patient-level analysis (n=10), no pairwise model difference remained statistically significant after Holm correction. Eunju Park, Uiwon Hwang
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp

☆ FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
Ching-Heng Cheng, Chia-Ming Lee, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Yu-Lun Liu, Chih-Chung Hsu
Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. It is inherently interactive: users try many focal points and blur strengths on one image, so each edit should be fast and change only the blur. Recent generative methods, however, rerun large diffusion models for every edit. We observe that the two sub-problems differ in kind: recovering the all-in-focus image is ill-posed and needs a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders every edit with a lightweight network. To address the ill-posed restoration, a one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. For precise control, the renderer is conditioned on an explicit defocus map and uses defocus-bias attention, which lets pixels at similar defocus share information without interference from pixels at other depths; in-focus content stays unchanged, and editing the map yields tilt-shift and two focal planes. To further test generalization to unseen cameras, we collect 3CReal, a three-camera benchmark of 89 pairs. FlashReFocus achieves the best perceptual fidelity for zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! and 3CReal, refocuses 148.3x faster than GenRefocus, and takes about half a second per further edit, 462x faster.

☆ The Optimal Ranking Tradeoffs Between Two Ranking Scores in Two-Class Classification
Sébastien Piérard, Adrien Deliège, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
The accuracy, true negative rate (negative class recall), true positive rate (positive class recall), negative predictive value (negative class precision), positive predictive value (positive class precision), class-specific intersections over unions, class-specific F-scores, Cohen's kappa, and balanced accuracy are scores that one intuitively wants to maximize when developing machine learning methods. However, they lead to different rankings of such methods. So, how can we establish a ranking that is an optimal tradeoff between any pair of these scores? It turns out that all these scores are special cases of ranking scores: a continuum of scores parameterized by the relative importance values assigned to the true negative, false positive, false negative, and true positive outcomes. Since all these scores are known to induce meaningful rankings, we seek the optimal tradeoffs among them. We consider the tradeoff between two scores to be optimal when it minimizes the Fréchet variance regarding the Kendall distance (also known as the bubble-sort distance) between rankings. For any given set of classifiers to rank, the optimal tradeoff lies at the center of the shortest (geodesic) path on the manifold of all rankings induced by the ranking scores. However, in the parameter space of the ranking scores, it is rarely achieved by averaging the importance values corresponding to the initial scores. In this paper, we present an exact analytical solution for determining a ranking score that is an optimal tradeoff for any given pair of initial scores, in the common case where the class priors are the same for all compared performances. We also experimentally investigate what happens when performance follows some distributions with fixed priors.

In this work, we revisit I2V immunization as reducing source-content preservation, shifting the focus from output degradation to weakening source-conditioned content propagation. To this end, we propose I2V-DETACH, an image immunization method that prevents unauthorized I2V generation through source grounding detachment. I2V models preserve source content by propagating source-image cues into video latents during denoising. Accordingly, I2V-DETACH disrupts this process in two complementary ways: it suppresses source-video grounding to reduce source cue propagation, and strengthens intra-video interactions to shift denoising toward video-side dynamics with reduced reliance on the source image. To obtain informative optimization signals, we initialize auxiliary video latents with source-oriented states that remain within the source-conditioned generation regime while deviating from source-preserving trajectories. Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion architectures show that I2V-DETACH substantially reduces source-content preservation, improves over prior immunization methods, and exhibits strong black-box transferability.

Relational out-of-distribution errors are easy to describe and hard to evaluate cleanly. An image may be natural, a caption may be fluent, and all mentioned objects may be common, yet the caption may describe the wrong relation in the image. Many evaluations intended to test this behavior can be solved without checking the pairing at all, because negatives differ in caption style, template, length, object frequency, or image statistics. The same contrast also gives a training loss for relational outlier exposure and a diagnostic for bilinear vision-language scores. Across synthetic controls, GQA, and COCO, cycles separate coarse image-caption matching from directional role-binding failures, while also identifying geometric size relations that remain strongly visible in global features. In a shortcut-contaminated COCO outlier-exposure stress test, a model selected by a near-perfect shortcut validation AUROC retains substantial relational signal but remains below cycle training on exact cycles; cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927. The main lesson is simple: to test whether a model understands a pairing, the benchmark should keep the parts fixed, change the pairing, and ask only about coupling. The official implementation is available online.

In this work, we explore a different direction for fast personalization in visual autoregressive models. The frozen generator subsequently predicts the remaining scales through bitwise self-correction for coherent refinement. Experiments on CSD-100 show that Kingfisher achieves strong content preservation and the highest style and text alignment among the evaluated methods, while reducing pair-specific preparation time by approximately 54x compared with diffusion-based methods and 7.5x compared with VAR-based alternatives. These results demonstrate that effective personalization can be achieved by directly manipulating the native scale-space representation of a frozen visual autoregressive generator.

The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.

For each detection, a simple training-free target-scene estimator produces branch-wise appearance reliability used across the two temporal roles of appearance: relative reliability regulates different identity branches, absolute reliability calibrates borderline candidates near the ReID acceptance boundary, and the same branch-wise reliability controls how strongly matched descriptors update historical appearance memory. The individual components are intentionally simple, focusing evaluation on reliability-controllable appearance organization rather than elaborate fusion or learned reliability-estimation modules. RCA-MOT sets new SOTA results on VT-MOT and UniRTL, improving the previous best HOTA by 5.402/6.075 points and IDF1 by 11.549/12.789 points, respectively, while post-hoc analyses further validate reliability as an informative control signal. Code will be released upon acceptance.

♻ ★ FaithfulFaces: Pose-Faithful Facial Identity Preservation for Text-to-Video Generation NeurIPS 2026
Yuanzhi Wang, Xuhua Ren, Jiaxiang Cheng, Bing Ma, Kai Yu, Sen Liang, Wenyue Li, Tianxiang Zheng, Qinglin Lu, Zhen Cui
Identity-preserving text-to-video generation (IPT2V) empowers users to produce diverse and imaginative videos with consistent human facial identity. Despite recent progress, existing methods often suffer from significant identity distortion under large facial pose variations or facial occlusions. In this paper, we propose FaithfulFaces, a pose-faithful facial identity preservation learning framework to improve IPT2V in complex dynamic scenes. The key of FaithfulFaces is a pose-shared identity aligner that refines and aligns facial poses across distinct views via a pose-shared dictionary and a pose variation-identity invariance constraint. By mapping single-view inputs into a global facial pose representation with explicit Euler angle embeddings, FaithfulFaces provides a pose-faithful facial prior that guides generative foundations toward robust identity-preserving generation. In particular, we develop a specialized pipeline to curate a high-quality video dataset featuring substantial facial pose diversity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FaithfulFaces achieves state-of-the-art performance, maintaining superior identity consistency and structural clarity even as pose changes and occlusions occur. Project Page: https://mdswyz.github.io/FaithfulFaces/

♻ ☆ Would you still call this Dax? Novel Visual References in VLMs and Humans EMNLP
Ada Defne Tür, Gaurav Kamath, Joyce Chai, Siva Reddy, Benno Krojer
Vision-language models (VLMs), like human learners, are frequently exposed to new visual concepts, but how they map novel visual references to language after exposure remains largely underexplored, particularly when those references contradict prior knowledge from pre-training. To study this, we present the Novel Visual References Dataset (NVRD): 19,176 images spanning 90 visual concepts across different levels of visual novelty, each with up to 20 increasingly perturbed versions of the original object to probe generalization. Unlike prior work on visual augmentations of familiar concepts, NVRD comprises entirely novel, open-ended stimuli constructed from scratch, mirroring how humans encounter genuinely new concepts. We evaluate 3 open- and 2 closed-source models alongside 2,400 human judgments for direct human-model comparison, and find that (i) models struggle to acquire novel concepts in-context when they contradict prior knowledge, and (ii) while models and humans show correlated sensitivity to visual perturbations, models significantly overgeneralize, extending learned labels to stimuli that humans reject. We contribute NVRD as a corpus and benchmark for research on visual concept learning in both humans and machines.

♻ ☆ Neural Block-wise Auto-exposure for Single-Shot High Dynamic Range Imaging
Zhengguo Li, Chaobing Zheng, Wei Wang
Block-wise varying exposures are effective for cap- turing appearance of a real-world high dynamic range (HDR) scene via a single-shot. However, brightness order reversal (BOR) artifacts, blocking artifacts and loss of details in highlight/shadow regions are possible issues for block-wise varying exposures. In this paper, a novel neural block-wise auto-exposure algorithm is proposed to address the issues. The proposed algorithm maps a temporary image and its exposure time to the exposure times of all non-overlapping 16 X 16 blocks. The temporary image can be either an sRGB or a raw image. Although the sRGB image is widely adopted in existing auto-exposure algorithms, exposure times of blocks in the highlight and shadow regions might not be accurately learned due to the limited radiance measurement capability of the sRGB image. This paper thus also explores the feasibility of temporary image as a raw image. Due to the better radiance measurement capability of the raw image, the exposure times of blocks are learned more accurately, and more details in the highlight/shadow regions of the real-world HDR scene are captured by the resultant HDR imaging system. Experiment results validate the proposed neural block-wise auto-exposure algorithm.
comment: High dynamic rang imaging, Single-shot, Block-wise, Auto-exposure, Neural network
♻ ☆ Dual-State Slot Attention: Decoupling Appearance and Identity for Video Object-Centric Learning
Sieu Tran, Duc Nguyen, Hao Vo, Khoa Vo, Ngan Le
Unsupervised video object-centric learning aims to decompose dynamic scenes into persistent, object-level representations without supervision. However, existing slot-based methods struggle to maintain stable object identity in challenging settings such as rapid motion and partial occlusion. First, they typically encode both the per-frame appearance of an object and its identity across frames in a single slot vector, creating an objective conflict that leads to slot swapping: reconstruction requires sensitivity to transient visual changes, whereas temporal consistency requires invariance to them. Second, the token renormalization used in Slot Attention can amplify weakly attending slots, allowing them to absorb tokens from other objects and destabilize slot-to-object correspondence. We propose Dual-State Slot Attention (DSSA), a fully self-supervised framework that addresses these limitations by separating appearance from identity and by reducing spurious updates from weakly matching slots. DSSA decomposes each slot into a local state for per-frame appearance and an identity state for temporally stable object information, thereby aligning reconstruction and temporal consistency with separate representations. The identity state is updated through a learned recurrent transition that acts as a temporal filter on the local state, while competition-modulated aggregation (CMA) down-weights updates from weakly matching slots and prevents them from absorbing tokens from other objects. Experiments on MOVi-C, MOVi-D, and YouTube-VIS demonstrate that DSSA consistently improves segmentation quality and temporal consistency over prior methods, while also yielding stronger downstream object recognition and video dynamics prediction. Code is available at \href{https://uark-aicv.github.io/dssa/}{\texttt{uark-aicv.github.io/dssa}}.

♻ ☆ Differentiable design of the PIAA-ZWFS: a flexible wavefront sensor that approaches the fundamental limit
A. K. Taras, S. Y. Haffert, L. Desdoigts
Extreme adaptive optics (AO) is necessary for high contrast astronomy at scales of the habitable zone of nearby systems. We seek to evaluate wavefront sensors that approach fundamental limits of wavefront sensing, enabling adaptive optics systems to run faster or on fainter targets. We present the phase-induced amplitude apodisation Zernike wavefront sensor (PIAA-ZWFS): an adaptation of the conventional Zernike wavefront sensor (ZWFS) that leverages lossless apodisation of the pupil to concentrate the starlight in the focal plane. We optimise and evaluate the sensor with a differentiable modelling framework, drawing on concepts from Bayesian experimental design to minimise the variance of a maximum likelihood estimator that uses the system in the high Strehl regime. Our architecture shows state-of-the-art performance in simulation for different apertures, bandwidths, photon fluxes and source sizes, closing the gap to the fundamental limit by a factor 10 (2.5) compared to the conventional ZWFS (optimised ZWFS) in a typical photon-limited case. For extended sources, we show that even an ideal point source sensor rapidly becomes sub-optimal, and our system outperforms it for stellar diameters larger than 0.8λ/D. We verify that these gains do not come at the cost of dynamic range with either linear or non-linear reconstructors. Finally, we present a proof that there must be a trade-off between the information gained about amplitude and phase errors for any wavefront sensor. The PIAA-ZWFS is a viable wavefront sensor operating near the fundamental sensitivity limits.

♻ ☆ Referring Multi-Object Tracking with Diverse Dynamic Expressions
Yani Zhang, Dongming Wu, Wencheng Han, Xingping Dong, Shengcai Liao, Bo Du
Referring understanding is a fundamental task that bridges natural language and visual content by localizing objects described in free-form expressions. However, existing works are constrained by limited language expressiveness, lacking the capacity to model object dynamics in spatial numbers and temporal states. To address these limitations, we introduce a new and general referring understanding task, termed referring multi-object tracking (RMOT). Its core idea is to employ a language expression as a semantic cue to guide the prediction of multi-object tracking, comprehensively accounting for variations in object quantity and temporal semantics. Along with RMOT, we introduce a RMOT benchmark named Refer-KITTI-V2, featuring scalable and diverse language expressions. To efficiently generate high-quality annotations covering object dynamics with minimal manual effort, we propose a semi-automatic labeling pipeline that formulates a total of 9,758 language prompts. In addition, we propose TempRMOT, an elegant end-to-end Transformer-based framework for RMOT. At its core is a query-driven Temporal Enhancement Module that represents each object as a Transformer query, enabling long-term spatial-temporal interactions with other objects and past frames to efficiently refine these queries. TempRMOT achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Refer-KITTI and Refer-KITTI-V2, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. The source code and dataset is available at https://github.com/zyn213/TempRMOT.
♻ ☆ BenthicDINO: Physics-Informed Self-Distillation for View-Invariant Side-Scan Sonar Representations
Taqi Hamoda, Hayat Rajani, Nuno Gracias
Automated interpretation of side-scan sonar (SSS) imagery is traditionally hindered by view-dependence, as recorded intensities inextricably conflate intrinsic seabed reflectivity with transient acquisition geometries and acoustic artifacts. To address this, we introduce BenthicDINO, a physics-informed self-supervised learning framework that decouples acquisition dynamics from seabed representations. Utilizing a ConvNeXt-v2 backbone, physics-guided augmentations, and an HSIC penalty, BenthicDINO explicitly enforces feature invariance to physical viewing parameters like slant range and incidence angle. Evaluations demonstrate exceptional data efficiency - achieving near-peak performance in benthic habitat mapping with only 10% of available labels - and strong cross-domain generalization, outperforming fully supervised baselines on the AI4Shipwrecks benchmark using frozen representations.
♻ ☆ NutriVision: Ingredient-Conditioned Fusion and Prediction for Single-Image Food Nutrition Estimation
Avinash Anand, Aman Kumar, Chaitanya Lakhchaura, Ashutosh Kumar, Akshita Abrol, Timothy Liu, Zhengkui Wang
Nutrition estimation is a fundamental task in consumer diet tracking, clinical dietetics, chronic disease management, sports and hospital nutrition, and broader food computing systems. The existing approaches have progressed along two largely separate axes, vision models that rely on calibrated RGB-depth captures and ingredient-aware methods that use textual cues but use limited multimodal fusion. We introduce NutriVision, an end-to-end framework that leverages visual geometry and ingredient semantics to estimate calories, mass, fat content, carbohydrates, and protein from a single RGB image and an optional ingredient list. It obtains the unavailable depth modality using DepthAnything-V3 and encodes ingredient descriptions using CLIP. It integrates three complementary mechanisms: (1) an \emph{Ingredient-Conditioned Frequency-Aligned Fusion Module (IC-FAFM)}, which uses textual guidance to reweight and align RGB-depth frequency components; (2) an \emph{Ingredient-Aware Mask-based Prediction Head (IA-MPH)}, whose gating and channel masks are conditioned on food identity; and (3) modality-specific \emph{Internal Semantic Modeling (ISM)} blocks. On the Nutrition5k dataset, NutriVision achieves a mean PMAE of $\mathbf{13.60\pm0.10\%}$, outperforming our IGSMNet implementation by $0.89$ percentage points and OmniFood8k by $2.90$ percentage points (both $p<0.001$). The module-level ablations identify the ingredient-aware prediction head as the primary architectural contributor, improving mean PMAE by $1.50\pm0.17$ percentage points ($p<0.001$). These results demonstrate that ingredient-conditioned prediction and frequency-aware RGB-depth fusion provide measurable gains for single-image nutrient estimation. More broadly, NutriVision offers a practical route toward nutrition-assessment systems that exploit geometric and semantic cues without requiring specialized depth-sensing hardware
♻ ☆ Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields
Jianqiang Wang, Junhui Hou, Siyu Ren, Weiyao Lin, Wenping Wang
Mesh texture compression typically relies on 2D UV atlases, whose chart discontinuities and mapping overhead can limit coding efficiency. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TexF, a surface-aligned texture field that organizes texture attributes in sparse voxels derived from the mesh surface. This representation supports high-resolution textures while preserving local 3D correlations for compression and enabling direct surface queries. For bitstream compression, TexF reuses established 3D attribute codecs, with voxel locations reconstructed from the decoded mesh without separate transmission. For GPU-resident compression, we develop 3DNTC, which combines quantized hash features with a lightweight decoder for random-access reconstruction at surface positions. Differentiable rendering enables image-space refinement of both voxel attributes and compressed neural fields. Experiments on the MPEG and AOM mesh compression benchmarks demonstrate improved average rate-distortion performance over representative UV-based methods for both bitstream and GPU-resident compression. 3DNTC also supports real-time rendering.

♻ ☆ Edit-Your-Interest: Efficient Video Editing via Feature Most-Similar Propagation
Yi Zuo, Zitao Wang, Lingling Li, Xu Liu, Fang Liu, Licheng Jiao
Text-to-image diffusion models have advanced video editing. However, existing video editing methods are limited by their high computational overhead and memory consumption. Furthermore, these approaches often sacrifice visual fidelity, leading to temporal inconsistencies and artifacts such as blurring and mosaic-like patterns. To address these dual challenges and strike a balance between computational efficiency and visual fidelity, we propose Edit-Your-Interest, a lightweight, text-driven, zero-shot video editing method. Edit-Your-Interest introduces a Spatio-Temporal Feature Memory bank (SFM) to cache spatial-attention features from previous frames under a fixed memory budget. The SFM maintains a representative candidate pool, reducing the computational overhead of full-sequence spatio-temporal modeling. To query this memory, we propose Feature Most-Similar Propagation (FMP), a similarity-based retrieval rule that propagates relevant cached tokens to the current frame. Together, SFM and FMP form a bounded-memory retrieval-based propagation design that improves temporal consistency while reducing blurring and mosaic-like artifacts. Finally, we introduce a feature-diversity-based SFM update algorithm to keep the memory representative and non-redundant throughout the video sequence. Furthermore, to enable precise object editing, we leverage cross-attention maps to automatically extract masks for the instances of interest. These masks are seamlessly integrated into the diffusion denoising process, enabling fine-grained control over target objects and allowing Edit-Your-Interest to perform highly accurate edits while robustly preserving the background integrity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Edit-Your-Interest outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both efficiency and visual fidelity. Project page: https://edit-your-interest.github.io/.

♻ ☆ Happy Young Women, Grumpy Old Men? Emotion-Driven Demographic Biases in Synthetic Face Generation
Mengting Wei, Aditya Gulati, Guoying Zhao, Nuria Oliver
Synthetic faces from text-to-image (T2I) models pervade digital media, yet their demographic biases under emotionally conditioned prompts remain poorly understood. We aim to systematically audit how emotionally conditioned prompts affect demographic and perceived-attractiveness biases in synthetic faces generated by T2I models, with particular attention to intersectional patterns and cross-ecosystem differences across model families. We audited eight (4 Western and 4 Chinese) T2I models and generated 56,000 faces under seven prompt conditions: a neutral baseline and six emotion conditions. We quantified biases in gender, race, age, and perceived attractiveness using information-theoretic divergence metrics. We further conducted intersectional analyses across combined demographic attributes and compared patterns between the Western and Chinese model groups to assess cross-ecosystem consistency and divergence in bias behavior. All models show strong overrepresentation of young faces, and most also overrepresent White-coded individuals. Intersectional analysis reveals compound underrepresentation or near-erasure of specific demographic combinations, such as young x female x Black faces, which are largely absent across models and are not captured by single-attribute audits. Emotion prompts act as additional demographic selectors: negatively valenced emotions (including sadness and fear) consistently shift outputs toward White, middle-aged, male-coded faces. This produces a valence-driven mapping that is also associated with lower perceived attractiveness in generated faces. These findings indicate that demographic bias in T2I face generation is both pervasive and shaped by emotional conditioning. They underscore the need for intersectional, emotion-conditioned, and multilingual demographic audits as part of standard pre-deployment evaluation practices.

♻ ☆ Visual Input and Its Framing Affect Undermine the Stability of Attribute-based Descriptions Produced by Large Vision-Language Models
Xiaomeng Wang, Martha Larson, Ping Mei Vogels, Zhengyu Zhao
Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are commonly prompted with text alone or together with an image. In this paper, we find a new aspect of LVLM vulnerability in its response robustness: adding an image can unexpectedly affect responses even when text prompts ask about a concept rather than the instance of the concept depicted in the image. For example, adding an image of an animal can change the generated attribute descriptions of its breed, and framing of the image further affects those changes. We study this new problem on seven LVLMs with image sets covering 30 animal breeds and eight food categories, using two types of framings that focus on the subject (subject-focused) or place it in a broader context (subject-in-situation). We draw the following main findings: (1) adding images increases physical-term proportions for animals (16.7\% $\to$ 32.8\%) and decreases sensory-term proportions for food (83.6\% $\to$ 73.2\%) among the most frequent terms, averaged over seven models and two framings on correctly recognized images. (2) attribute-term distributions differ significantly between the two framing types for 41.4\% of animal and 71.4\% of food model--concept pairs, with generally higher physical-term proportions for animals and sensory-term proportions for food under subject-focused than subject-in-situation framing.
♻ ☆ Through the PRISm: Importance-Aware Scene Graphs for Semantic Image Retrieval
Dimitrios Georgoulopoulos, Nikolaos Chaidos, Angeliki Dimitriou, Giorgos Stamou
Web-based visual search increasingly handles queries driven by semantic intent, focusing on what is happening in an image rather than merely what it looks like. While global embeddings from vision-language models capture overall appearance, they often blur fine-grained relational structure. Conversely, scene graphs make these relationships explicit, but generating them automatically for unannotated web images produces dense, noisy graphs that retain every detected entity and relation regardless of relevance. To address this, we introduce PRISm (Pruning-based Image Retrieval via Importance Prediction on Semantic Graphs), an image-to-image retrieval framework that learns to focus on what matters in a scene. PRISm employs an Importance Prediction Module, supervised by caption-derived relevance strictly during training, to score and prune non-essential objects and triplets. An Edge-Aware Contextual GNN then aggregates relation conditioned neighbor messages, fusing the refined graph with global visual features into a single, index-ready embedding per image. On PSG, PRISm outperforms the strongest baseline by points in MAP@1. Furthermore, on Flickr with machine-generated scene graphs and captions, PRISm remains best on top-1 metrics, while adding only 33,ms per query beyond scene graph generation.

♻ ☆ Learnable Spectral Activations
Tamir Shor, Or Litany, Alex Bronstein
Implicit neural representations (INRs) are shaped by the spectral structure induced by their input encodings and activation functions. Existing methods improve fitting primarily by modifying which frequencies are available to the network, through coordinate encodings or periodic nonlinearities. However, frequency access is not the only bottleneck: signals with localized or spatially varying structure require the network to efficiently compose frequencies into multi-harmonic internal responses. We introduce learnable spectral activations (LSA), which replace fixed neuron-level nonlinearities with a residual truncated Fourier series whose harmonic amplitudes are learned during training. LSA does not expand the asymptotic function class. Instead, it changes the factorization of the representation: linear weights select features while activation coefficients control spectral shaping, and the two are updated by separate gradients. Because the activation output is affine in the coefficients given fixed pre-activations, spectral tuning becomes a more direct subproblem compared to architectures where it is entangled with feature selection. Empirically, this factorization concentrates more target-signal energy in the leading eigenmodes of the neural tangent kernel, consistent with improved optimization behavior. Across audio, image, neural radiance field, and neural acoustic field tasks, LSA also improves reconstruction quality.
♻ ☆ CorrelationFlow: A Training-Free Geometric Approach for LiDAR Scene Flow Estimation
Minh-Quan Dao, Yancong Lin, Shiming Wang, Julie Stephany Berrio Perez, Holger Caesar
LiDAR scene flow is the task of estimating point-wise motion from sequential point clouds. It is essential for autonomous driving, as it provides critical information about moving objects and their trajectories. In recent years, unsupervised methods have gained significant traction by eliminating the need for expensive point-wise annotations. However, despite incremental performance improvements, these methods uniformly rely on a single paradigm: training feed-forward networks through optimizing a loss function based on the Chamfer distance, a framework that inherently limits their progression. This paper presents CorrelationFlow, a new paradigm that reformulates LiDAR scene flow as a correlation maximization problem between Bird's-Eye View (BEV) images. Instead of using learnable parameters, our approach employs a chain of image processing operations to solve this problem. The learning-free nature of CorrelationFlow enables strong generalization across diverse domains. This capability is demonstrated by the second-place ranking in the unsupervised track of the Argoverse 2 Scene Flow Challenge at CVPR 2026, which featured a test set spanning five datasets that cover varied vehicle platforms and environments. Our results show that this classical, model-based approach can match or even surpass the performance of learning-based methods, thereby opening a new direction for unsupervised LiDAR scene flow research. The source code will be released.
♻ ☆ GroundAnything: Reconciling Parallel Decoding with Precise Visual Grounding at Flash Speed
Qize Yu, Lianrui Fan, Bowen Ping, Xini Ding, Zetian Song, Junbo Niu, Kaixuan Wang, Tianxing Chen, Yue Chen, Minghua He, Yuran Wang, Jie Huang, Haojun Zhang, Min Chen, Hao Li, Wenxuan Song, Ruihai Wu, Xianming Liu, Shilong Liu, Shuchang Zhou, Ping Luo, Shiyu Huang
Autoregressive (AR) grounding models serialize spatial predictions, introducing sequential latency and imposing a causal order on output tokens. We view grounding as visual evidence extraction: objects, locations, and spatial relations are jointly constrained by the image and query, yet their dependencies do not imply an intrinsic left-to-right generation order. This distinction makes bidirectional diffusion a natural fit, allowing spatial hypotheses to emerge in parallel and be jointly refined through iterative denoising. We introduce GroundAnything, a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that reconciles fast parallel decoding with precise localization through blockwise denoising. Training combines grounding pretraining from public datasets and dedicated data engines, direct AR-to-diffusion conversion with joint AR and diffusion objectives, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO-based reinforcement post-training. Across 30 grounding benchmarks, our autoregressive variant, GroundAnything-VLM, establishes a new overall state of the art among similarly sized models at 72.42%, remaining competitive with GPT-6 Astra (71.35%). With entropy-guided decoding, GroundAnything also surpasses the prior state of the art at this scale, averaging 61.75% versus 53.32% for the fast MTP-based LocateAnything model. We further explore decoding strategies, showing that an optional self-speculative mode achieves a $4.51\times$ speedup over the AR counterpart with a 0.74 percentage-point drop in COCO F1mIoU. Infrastructure experiments show that progressive inference optimizations translate parallel decoding into practical speedups. These support efficient visual grounding in latency-sensitive real-world systems.

♻ ☆ GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives
Qize Yu, Lianrui Fan, Boyu Chen, Jiaqi Liang, Xini Ding, Yue Chen, Zetian Song, Yuran Wang, Yi Zou, Kaixuan Wang, Tianxing Chen, Wenxuan Song, Bohan Zhou, Mingleyang Li, Siqiao Huang, Yuqi Ye, Caigao Jiang, Wei Wei, Ruihai Wu, Hang Zhang, Yixiao Ge, Shuchang Zhou, Shilong Liu, Xianming Liu, Ping Luo, Shiyu Huang
Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control. Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines. Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%). As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. On RoboTwin 2.0, it outperforms every mainstream backbone we evaluate in all four out-of-distribution settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest backbone. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%. On nuScenes, used as the visual backbone, GroundingPI attains an average open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Downstream autonomous driving and robotic manipulation improve as the pretraining is scaled. Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.

♻ ☆ Scalable Adaptation of 3D Geometric Foundation Models via Weak Supervision from Internet Video NeurIPS 2026
Zihui Gao, Ke Liu, Donny Y. Chen, Duochao Shi, Guosheng Lin, Jia-Wang Bian, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
Geometric foundation models show promise in 3D reconstruction. However, their progress is severely constrained by the scarcity of diverse, large-scale 3D annotations. While static-scene Internet videos are abundant and diverse, utilizing them as a scaling source for geometric learning is challenging due to the absence of ground-truth geometry and the presence of observational noise. To address this, we propose SAGE, a framework for Scalable Adaptation of GEometric foundation models from raw video streams. SAGE leverages a hierarchical mining pipeline to transform videos into training trajectories and hybrid supervisions: (1) Informative training trajectory selection; (2) Sparse Geometric Anchoring via SfM point clouds for global structural guidance; and (3) Dense Differentiable Consistency via 3D Gaussian rendering for multi-view constraints. Besides, we also introduce a regularization strategy that replays a small fraction of supervised data to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Applied to two architecturally distinct backbones, SAGE reduces Chamfer Distance on unseen benchmarks (7Scenes, TUM-RGBD, Matterport3D) by 20-42% with MV-DUSt3R and consistently improves VGGT. SAGE establishes Internet video as a viable and scalable adaptation source for geometric foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/SAGE.

♻ ☆ MeshSuite: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering
Kaixuan Zhang, Minxian Li, Mingwu Ren, Xiatian Zhu
Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine deployment and Non-Engine Render in triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering. MeshSuite evaluates two deployment settings: Standard Deployment, using an opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; and Dedicated Deployment, using method-specific engine implementations to preserve appearance and compositing features. For mesh splatting, we also audit exported surfaces for topological and geometric integrity as downstream graphics assets. Our results show that engine deployment reduces image quality in both settings; among evaluated methods, MeshSplatting degrades least under Standard Deployment. Dedicated Deployment preserves most fidelity at roughly 5-33x the runtime of Standard Deployment across two deployment datasets. For mesh splatting, explicit connectivity and shared indexing remain limited: shared vertex indexing alone guarantees neither manifoldness nor global connectivity. These findings show that rasterizability is only part of graphics readiness and underscore the need to assess engine deployment. Project page: https://surrey-up-lab.github.io/MeshSuite.
♻ ☆ OMEGA-Avatar: One-shot Modeling of 360° Gaussian Avatars
Zehao Xia, Yiqun Wang, Zhengda Lu, Kai Liu, Jun Xiao, Peter Wonka
Creating high-fidelity, animatable 3D avatars from a single image remains a formidable challenge. We identified three desirable attributes of avatar generation: 1) the method should be feed-forward, 2) model a 360° full-head, and 3) should be animation-ready. However, current work addresses only two of the three points simultaneously. To address these limitations, we propose OMEGA-Avatar, the first feed-forward framework that simultaneously generates a generalizable, 360°-complete, and animatable 3D Gaussian head from a single image. Starting from a feed-forward and animatable framework, we address the 360° full-head avatar generation problem with two novel components. First, to overcome poor hair modeling in full-head avatar generation, we introduce a semantic-aware mesh deformation module that integrates multi-view normals to optimize a FLAME head with hair while preserving its topology structure. Second, to enable effective feed-forward decoding of full-head features, we propose a multi-view feature splatting module that constructs a shared canonical UV representation from features across multiple views through differentiable bilinear splatting, hierarchical UV mapping, and visibility-aware fusion. This approach preserves both global structural coherence and local high-frequency details across all viewpoints, ensuring 360° consistency without per-instance optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OMEGA-Avatar achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforming existing baselines in 360° full-head completeness while robustly preserving identity across different viewpoints.

♻ ★ IMPLICIT-Bench: Stereotyped Defaults and Prompt Following in Text-to-Image Generation
Yue Dai, Ziyang Liu, Marc Cheong, Caren Han
Text-to-image (T2I) models often produce stereotypical images when stereotype-relevant attributes are left unspecified. We ask whether explicit requests can overcome these defaults, especially when the requested attribute contradicts the stereotype. We introduce \mbox{IMPLICIT-Bench}, a challenge benchmark of 1,831 prompt triplets built on a bias knowledge graph (KG) of stereotypes recorded in StereoSet and CrowS-Pairs. Each triplet describes one scene with a neutral prompt, a stereotype prompt, and an anti-stereotype prompt. The neutral prompt measures the model's default, and the two explicit prompts measure whether the model can follow a request on either side of the stereotype. On this benchmark, Qwen-Image depicts the stereotype in 52\% of neutral images and the anti-stereotype in 5\%. On both Qwen-Image and Stable Diffusion~3, explicit requests that contradict this default succeed far less often than requests that agree with it. Where Qwen-Image's default is strongest, explicitly requesting the stereotype succeeds in 97\% of cases, whereas requesting the anti-stereotype succeeds in only 54\%. In these scenes, 31\% of the images for anti-stereotype requests show the stereotypical attribute instead. We further test whether prompt rewriting and embedding steering can reduce the default on neutral prompts. With the prompt's own KG unit, the best configurations improve a combined bias and alignment score by up to 9.5 points, and with a unit retrieved from the bias KG, by at most 2.9. Debiasing thus depends on knowing which stereotype a prompt evokes.
♻ ☆ FlexPainter: Flexible and Multi-View Consistent Texture Generation
Dongyu Yan, Leyi Wu, Jiantao Lin, Luozhou Wang, Tianshuo Xu, Zhifei Chen, Zhen Yang, Lie Xu, Shunsi Zhang, Yingcong Chen
Texture map production is an important part of 3D modeling and determines the rendering quality. Recently, diffusion-based methods have opened a new way for texture generation. However, restricted control flexibility and limited prompt modalities may prevent creators from producing desired results. Furthermore, inconsistencies between generated multi-view images often lead to poor texture generation quality. To address these issues, we introduce \textbf{FlexPainter}, a novel texture generation pipeline that enables flexible multi-modal conditional guidance and achieves highly consistent texture generation. A shared conditional embedding space is constructed to perform flexible aggregation between different input modalities. Utilizing such embedding space, we present an image-based CFG method to decompose structural and style information, achieving reference image-based stylization. Leveraging the 3D knowledge within the image diffusion prior, we first generate multi-view images simultaneously using a grid representation to enhance global understanding. Meanwhile, we propose a view synchronization and adaptive weighting module during diffusion sampling to further ensure local consistency. Finally, a 3D-aware texture completion model combined with a texture enhancement model is used to generate seamless, high-resolution texture maps. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both flexibility and generation quality.
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures in main paper, 8 pages, 9 figures in supplementary
♻ ☆ Handwritten Text Recognition Lives in the High-Pixel Variance Subspace NeurIPS 2026
Carlos Garrido-Munoz, Jorge Calvo-Zaragoza
In self-supervised pretraining for Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR), pixel reconstruction methods outperform contrastive methods, unlike in natural-image classification. We argue that this difference follows from where discriminative signal lies in pixel space: for HTR, it is concentrated in high-variance directions and largely absent from low-variance ones. This predicts that objectives preserving high-variance pixel content will transfer best. We test six SSL methods from three families (pixel-grounded MIM, JEPA, and contrastive) under matched encoder, data, and evaluation protocols on six handwriting benchmarks across five languages. With full labels, pixel-groundrounded SSL achieves the lowest CER on every benchmark and both frozen probes, exposes per-position character information that other families recover only through the readout, and is the only family to benefit from pretraining on real handwriting. Pixel-grounded representations are also more label efficient. Across datasets, encoder alignment with the high-variance pixel subspace predicts CER within every method. With a pretrained LLM decoder, a frozen pixel-grounded encoder is competitive with fully fine-tuned supervised baselines; full fine-tuning achieves the lowest mean CER and ranks first or second on every benchmark. These results show that the value of pixel reconstruction depends on where discriminative signal lies in the input.
comment: Accepted at 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
♻ ☆ Beyond Generation: Using Multimodal LLMs as Detectors of LLM-Generated Deepfake Facial Images
Olivia Salamon, Virginia N. L. Franqueira, Shujun Li
As image generation models become increasingly capable of producing highly realistic content, traditional forensic techniques are struggling to keep up. This paper investigates whether MLLMs can instead be used as a form of forensic analysis by identifying synthetic media. Specifically, the study aims to determine whether these models detect fake images by recognising physical inconsistencies, or whether they rely on digital artefacts such as embedded watermarks. Six MLLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5, Gemini 3, and Seed 1.6) are benchmarked using a dataset of 400 images. Fifty images are authentic photographs, while the remaining 350 are generated using seven leading image models: Gemini 3, Gemini 2.5, Flux.2 Pro, GPT-Image-1, GPT-Image-1.5, Seedream 4.0, and Seedream 4.5. The evaluation is structured in three stages: single-image classification, pairwise comparison, and a focused "self-detection" experiment on Gemini. Several MLLMs achieved a high detection accuracy, with GPT-5.2 reaching a peak of 97.9% in the pairwise experiment, against specific generators and an overall mean pairwise accuracy of 82.5% by identifying structural or physical inconsistencies within images. However, results from the self-detection experiment indicate that the presence of invisible SynthID watermarks leads to a 10% reduction in Gemini's detection accuracy compared to the clean control group. One possible explanation is that SynthID embedding reduces some of the visible artefacts the models rely on for detection. These results imply that MLLMs can detect structural artefacts without relying on watermarks, but performance varies substantially across model generations. The findings also suggest that SynthID embedding may suppress some of the structural artefacts used during detection.
♻ ☆ Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark
Xudong Cai, Ruijie Zhu, Haoliang Shang, Ruining Li, Marc Pollefeys, Shangzhe Wu, Andrea Vedaldi, Chuanxia Zheng
In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.
comment: https://physicalvision.github.io/artisan/
♻ ☆ Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
Stavros Nousias, Akis Nousias, Konstantinos Gkrispanis
Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31% and interior mean squared error by 47%.
♻ ★ Mitigating Task Objective Conflicts for Continual Learning in Unified Multimodal Models
Jiaxing Zhang, Hao Tang
Recent advances in unified autoregressive (AR) models have enabled multimodal understanding (MMU) and text-to-image generation (T2I) within a single architecture. However, in continual learning settings, their divergent objectives can induce task interference, hindering knowledge preservation and adaptation to new tasks. In this work, we investigate \textbf{T}ask \textbf{O}bjective \textbf{C}onflict (TOC) through theoretical and empirical analyses, revealing conflicting optimization directions at the task level but complementary interactions at the token level. These findings suggest that continual adaptation requires mitigating task interference while preserving beneficial cross-task knowledge sharing. To this end, we propose \textbf{UniDecouple}, a selective decoupling framework based on a \textbf{T}ask-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{M}ixture-\textbf{o}f-\textbf{E}xperts (TA-MoE) architecture. Specifically, UniDecouple retains shared attention layers to preserve common contextual dependencies while introducing task-specific feed-forward network (FFN) experts to mitigate optimization conflicts. Furthermore, hierarchical expert routing enables adaptive expert selection, while hybrid expert collaboration leverages shared experts to facilitate cross-task knowledge transfer. A two-stage training strategy further balances task specialization and coordinated adaptation. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that UniDecouple improves both multimodal understanding and image generation performance under a comparable per-token activation budget, achieving a favorable balance between knowledge preservation and task adaptation in continual learning.
♻ ★ SpaceCast-Bench: Evaluating Predictive Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
Hongxing Li, Jinyue Su, Dingming Li, Wenqi Zhang, Weiming Lu, Jun Xiao, Yueting Zhuang, Yongliang Shen
Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks mainly test spatial perception: reading off relations already visible in the input. Yet real-world spatial intelligence demands predictive spatial reasoning: constructing a scene from observations, anticipating how an intervention changes it, and reasoning about the unseen outcome. We introduce SpaceCast-Bench, the first benchmark to directly and diagnostically evaluate this capability. Built around an observe-transform-infer framework, its 3,862 questions from 182 real-world scenes span 16 task types at three levels: static perception, local prediction, and global prediction, progressively requiring scene understanding, spatial state updating, and relational inference over unobserved outcomes. Evaluating 21 models exposes a stark gap: the strongest model reaches only 58.0% against 87.2% human performance, while spatially specialized models remain near random chance. Controlled analyses further reveal that bridge views are critical for integrating distributed observations, and that explicit 3D evidence benefits models more reliably than generated outcome images or videos. Fine-tuning on our programmatically generated data lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 34.0% to 65.7% with macro-average gains across six out-of-domain benchmarks.
